analog signal: A signal with many levels of intensity over a period of time (continuous). **Analog data** is continuous information such as sound. See [Data and signals](#/comp3721-w2/data-and-signals).
digital signal: A signal with a limited number of defined values, often 0 and 1. **Digital data** has discrete states (1s and 0s in memory). Most digital signals are nonperiodic, so they are described by **bit rate** rather than frequency. See [Data and signals](#/comp3721-w2/data-and-signals).
periodic: A signal that completes a pattern (a **cycle**) and repeats it every **period** $T$ seconds. In data communications we commonly use periodic analog signals and nonperiodic digital signals. See [Data and signals](#/comp3721-w2/data-and-signals).
sine wave: The most fundamental periodic analog signal, described by peak amplitude $A$, frequency $f$ and phase $\phi$: $s(t) = A\sin(2\pi f t + \phi)$. A **simple** sine wave cannot be decomposed; a **composite** signal is made of several. See [Sine wave](#/comp3721-w2/sine-wave).
A|peak amplitude: The absolute value of the signal's highest intensity, proportional to the energy it carries; measured in volts. Home voltage peaks at about $120\sqrt{2} \approx 170$ V. See [Sine wave](#/comp3721-w2/sine-wave).
f|frequency: The number of cycles completed in 1 second, in hertz (Hz = cycles per second); the rate of change with respect to time. $f = 1/T$. Independent of the transmission medium. See [Sine wave](#/comp3721-w2/sine-wave).
T|period: The time, in seconds, a signal needs to complete one full cycle. $T = 1/f$; 60 Hz gives 16.7 ms. See [Sine wave](#/comp3721-w2/sine-wave).
φ|phi|phase: The position of the waveform relative to time 0, in degrees or radians ($360° = 2\pi$ rad). $A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$ is shifted left by $\phi/\omega$; $-\phi$ shifts right. An offset of 1/9 cycle is $40° = 0.698$ rad. See [Phase](#/comp3721-w2/phase).
ω|omega: Angular frequency, $\omega = 2\pi f$ radians per second, so $s(t) = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$. See [Phase](#/comp3721-w2/phase).
λ|lambda|wavelength: The distance a simple signal travels in one period: $\lambda = c/f = c \cdot T$, where $c$ is the propagation speed of the medium. Depends on both frequency and medium; usually quoted in micrometres for light in fibre (red light: 0.75 μm). See [Wavelength](#/comp3721-w2/wavelength).
c|propagation speed: How fast a signal moves through a medium: $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s for light in a vacuum, lower in air, even lower in cable. See [Wavelength](#/comp3721-w2/wavelength).
Fourier analysis|Fourier: Any composite signal is a combination of simple sine waves with different frequencies, peak amplitudes and phases. Periodic composites decompose into discrete frequencies (harmonics); nonperiodic ones into a continuous range. See [Composite signals](#/comp3721-w2/composite-bandwidth).
harmonic|fundamental frequency: The sine waves a composite periodic signal decomposes into: the **fundamental frequency** (first harmonic) $f$, then integer multiples such as the third harmonic $3f$ and ninth harmonic $9f$. See [Composite signals](#/comp3721-w2/composite-bandwidth).
B|bandwidth: Of a composite signal: the difference between the highest and lowest frequencies it contains, $B = f_{high} - f_{low}$. With the middle frequency $(f_{high} + f_{low})/2$ you can solve for either end. See [Composite signals](#/comp3721-w2/composite-bandwidth).
bit rate: The number of bits sent per second (bps); the way digital signals are described since most are nonperiodic. Bit duration $= 1/\text{bit rate}$. See [Digital signals](#/comp3721-w2/digital-signals).
bit length: The distance one bit occupies on the transmission medium: propagation speed × bit duration (1 Mbps at $2 \times 10^{8}$ m/s gives 200 m). See [Digital signals](#/comp3721-w2/digital-signals).
L|level: A specific state or value a digital signal can have at a point in time. $L$ levels need $⌈\log_{2} L⌉$ bits per signal element: 4 levels need 2 bits, 11 levels need 4. See [Digital signals](#/comp3721-w2/digital-signals).
bps: Bits per second, the unit of bit rate. 1 536 000 bps = 1.536 Mbps. See [Digital signals](#/comp3721-w2/digital-signals).
